label: TS-01
title: TypeScript Definition

choices.text: A syntactic superset of JavaScript that adds static types
A CSS framework for web apps

explanation: TypeScript extends JavaScript syntax with a static type system.
prompt: What is TypeScript?

label: TS-02
title: Main Goal

choices.text: Catch errors early through compile-time type checking
Run directly in the browser without JavaScript

explanation: TypeScript improves reliability by checking types before runtime.
prompt: Why is TypeScript designed for better developer efficiency?

label: TS-03
title: Transpilation Output

choices.text: It transpiles to plain JavaScript that runs anywhere JavaScript runs
It compiles to machine code only for Windows
It runs only in Deno and nowhere else

explanation: TypeScript emits JavaScript, so it works in browsers and Node.js.
prompt: What happens to TypeScript code before execution?

label: TS-04
title: Checking .js Files

choices.text: Yes, TypeScript can type-check plain .js files when enabled
No, TypeScript only checks .ts files and ignores .js completely
Only if Babel is used instead of tsc

explanation: TypeScript supports checking JavaScript files with proper configuration.
prompt: Can TypeScript check inconsistencies in JavaScript code?

label: TS-05
title: JS Type Checking Setup

choices.text: Use only ESLint and no TypeScript config

explanation: JSDoc annotations plus checkJs enable static checks in .js files.
prompt: Which combination enables type checking in JavaScript files?

label: TS-06
title: Gradual Typing
explanation: TypeScript supports incremental adoption instead of full rewrites.
prompt: What is a practical way to adopt TypeScript in an existing JS project?

explanation: Transpile output is controlled through compiler options in tsconfig.

label: TS-08

explanation: The target setting belongs under compilerOptions in tsconfig.
prompt: Where is the TypeScript transpile target configured?

TypeScript parses CSS and emits HTML
TypeScript parses SQL and emits JSON
TypeScript only lints files without output

JavaScript is static; TypeScript is dynamic
Both are purely dynamic with no checks

explanation: This is the core contrast highlighted in the notes.

label: TS-12
title: Compile-Time Checking

choices.text: Types are checked before running the code
Types are checked only after deployment
Types are checked only in the browser console

choices.text: Disallows unreachable code when set to false
Enables dead code execution at runtime

choices.text: Add a breakpoint, open Debug panel, create launch.json, select Node.js
Only run npm install to debug
Use browser-only breakpoints for Node apps

explanation: The provided launch config uses node launch mode.

label: TS-26
title: JavaScript Built-in Types
explanation: These six were listed as JavaScript built-in types in the markdown.

label: TS-27
title: TypeScript Extended Types
explanation: These are the TypeScript-extended types listed in the lesson.
prompt: Select all TypeScript extended types from the notes.

label: TS-28
title: Explicit Typing

choices.text: You explicitly declare a variable's type
Types are assigned only at runtime

explanation: Explicit typing means writing type annotations yourself.
prompt: What does explicit typing mean in TypeScript?

label: TS-29
title: Type Inference

choices.text: TypeScript infers types from assigned values
Type inference works only for functions

explanation: Inference reduces manual annotations in many cases.
prompt: What is type inference in TypeScript?

label: TS-30
title: Tuple Concept

choices.text: A typed array with predefined length and index types
A dynamic object with unknown keys
A function that returns two values only

explanation: Tuples are fixed-position, fixed-type arrays.
prompt: Which statement best describes a TypeScript tuple?

label: TS-31
title: Tuple Safety Caveat

choices.text: Indexes 3+ may lose strict tuple safety when pushing new values
Tuples always reject push at compile time in all cases
Tuple values must all be strings

explanation: The notes highlight this practical tuple limitation.
prompt: What caution is shown in the tuple example?

label: TS-32
title: Enum Meaning

choices.text: An enum is a list of related constants
An enum is a runtime array method
An enum is a TypeScript package manager
An enum is a markdown syntax feature

explanation: Enums group named constant values.
prompt: What is an enum in TypeScript?

label: TS-33
title: const enum Benefit

choices.text: Compiler can generate more optimized code
It enables dynamic enum members at runtime

explanation: The lesson states const enums help optimization.
prompt: Why might you use `const enum`?

label: TS-34
title: Type Alias Definition

choices.text: A custom name for a type
A compiler option for source maps

explanation: Type aliases define types with custom names.
prompt: What does a TypeScript type alias allow you to define?

label: TS-35
title: Interface Scope

choices.text: Interfaces can only describe primitive numbers
Interfaces are only used in tsconfig.json

explanation: The notes describe interfaces as similar to type aliases, except focused on object types.
prompt: What are TypeScript interfaces mainly designed to describe?

label: TS-36
title: Type Alias Flexibility
explanation: The lesson lists type aliases as flexible enough for primitives, unions, intersections, tuples, mapped types, and functions.
prompt: Select all examples of things type aliases can represent.

label: TS-37
title: Interface Strengths

choices.text: Can be extended or implemented cleanly

explanation: These are the interface strengths called out in the lesson.
prompt: Select the core advantages of interfaces mentioned in the notes.

label: TS-38
title: Union Types

choices.text: A type that can be one of several types
A type that must contain all properties from every type
A type that disables type checking
A type that only accepts null

explanation: Union types allow a value to be one of multiple possible types.
prompt: What does a union type represent?

label: TS-39
title: Intersection Types

choices.text: A type that combines properties of multiple types
A type that randomly chooses one possible type
A type that can only hold string literals
A type that removes all object properties

explanation: An intersection such as A & B must satisfy both A and B.
prompt: What does an intersection type do?

label: TS-40
title: Literal Types
explanation: The lesson lists string, number, and boolean literal types.
prompt: Which literal type categories are available in TypeScript?

label: TS-41
title: Template Literal Types

choices.text: They create string types based on patterns
They create HTML templates at runtime

explanation: Template literal types let you model string patterns such as `/api/${string}`.
prompt: What are template literal types used for?

label: TS-42
title: Type Narrowing

choices.text: Refining a broad type to a more specific type inside a conditional block
Deleting all union members from a type
Changing a runtime value into another value

explanation: Type narrowing lets TypeScript understand a more specific type after checks such as typeof.
prompt: What is type narrowing?

label: TS-43
title: Narrowing Techniques
explanation: The lesson lists typeof, instanceof, user-defined guards, and discriminated unions as narrowing techniques.
prompt: Select all type narrowing techniques mentioned in the notes.

label: TS-44
title: Discriminated Unions

choices.text: A shared literal field that identifies the current union member
A field that stores any runtime value without checks
A field that must always be named id

explanation: Discriminated unions commonly use one shared literal field, such as state, to narrow the possible type.
prompt: What makes a discriminated union work?

label: TS-45
title: strictNullChecks

choices.text: null and undefined must be explicitly included in a type when needed
null becomes assignable to every number
undefined is removed from JavaScript output

explanation: With strictNullChecks enabled, null and undefined are not assignable unless the type says so.
prompt: What does `strictNullChecks` enforce?

label: TS-46
title: Handling Nullable Values

choices.text: Use union types to include null or undefined
Disable TypeScript for the whole project

explanation: The lesson recommends explicit unions, optional chaining, and nullish coalescing for null or undefined values.
prompt: Select the recommended ways to deal with null and undefined values.

label: TS-47
title: Optional Chaining

choices.text: Safely accesses a property when the value before it might be null or undefined
Forces a value to be non-null at runtime
Converts undefined into an empty string

explanation: Optional chaining prevents crashes while accessing nested values that may be null or undefined.
prompt: What does optional chaining do?

label: TS-48
title: Optional Chaining Forms
explanation: The notes show optional property access, optional element access, and optional call.
prompt: Select the optional chaining forms shown in the lesson.

label: TS-49
title: Nullish Coalescing

choices.text: It returns the right-hand value only when the left-hand value is null or undefined
It returns the right-hand value for every falsy value
It removes undefined from all object properties

explanation: `??` is a null-or-undefined fallback, not a general falsy fallback.
prompt: How does the nullish coalescing operator `??` behave?

label: TS-50
title: Nullish Assignment
explanation: The assignment version `value ??= 10` is equivalent to `value = value ?? 10`.
prompt: What is `value ??= 10` equivalent to?

label: TS-51
title: Type Assertion

choices.text: It tells the compiler to treat a value as a specific type without changing the runtime value
It converts the runtime value into the asserted type
It checks values from an API at runtime
It only works in JavaScript files

explanation: The lesson emphasizes that `as` does not perform conversion.
prompt: What does a TypeScript type assertion do?

label: TS-52
title: Assertion Syntax

choices.text: Angle-bracket syntax is the only valid syntax
Assertions are only allowed in comments

explanation: The notes show both forms, but identify `as` as the modern standard.
prompt: Which type assertion syntax is described as the modern standard?

label: TS-53
title: The any Type

choices.text: It can lead to runtime errors TypeScript is meant to prevent
It forces stricter narrowing before use

explanation: The lesson warns that `any` opts out of checking and can hide errors.
prompt: Why is using `any` not recommended?

label: TS-54
title: Implicit any

choices.text: It occurs when TypeScript cannot infer a type and no explicit annotation is provided
It occurs only when a variable is set to null
It is required for every function parameter
It converts unknown into any automatically

explanation: Implicit any can be caught with explicit annotations or `noImplicitAny`.
prompt: When does implicit `any` occur?

label: TS-55
title: The unknown Type

choices.text: It forces type checks or narrowing before using the value
It bypasses the type checker like any
It means the value can never exist

explanation: `unknown` is safer than `any` because you must narrow before use.
prompt: Why is `unknown` safer than `any`?

label: TS-56
title: The never Type

choices.text: It represents values that should not exist or code paths that cannot produce a value
It represents any possible runtime value

explanation: `never` is useful for functions that always throw, infinite loops, and exhausted branches.
prompt: What does the `never` type represent?

label: TS-57
title: never Use Cases

choices.text: Functions that always throw an error
Branches where all possibilities have been excluded
Variables that should accept every possible value

explanation: The notes describe these as cases where `never` applies.
prompt: Select the valid use cases for the `never` type.

label: TS-58
title: Utility Types
explanation: The lesson lists Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, and Omit as built-in utility types.
prompt: Select the TypeScript utility types listed in the notes.

label: TS-59
title: Partial Utility
explanation: `Partial<T>` makes every property in `T` optional.
prompt: What does `Partial<T>` do?

label: TS-60
title: Record Utility

choices.text: Creates a type with keys K and values of type T
Gets the return type of a function

explanation: `Record<K, T>` is useful for maps such as configuration or status objects.
prompt: What does `Record<K, T>` create?

label: TS-61
title: Function Utility Types
explanation: The lesson includes ReturnType, Parameters, ConstructorParameters, and InstanceType for function and constructor type work.
prompt: Select the utility types related to function or constructor types.

label: TS-62
title: Type Guards

choices.text: A function returning a predicate such as `user is Admin`
A function that removes all runtime checks
A tsconfig option for emitting declarations
A JSON schema generated from TypeScript

explanation: The notes show a user-defined guard like `isAdmin(user): user is Admin`.
prompt: What is a user-defined type guard?

label: TS-63
title: Conditional Types

choices.text: They create different types based on a condition
They run if statements at runtime
They prevent generic types from being used

explanation: Conditional types use a condition such as `T extends "error" ? A : B` to choose a type.
prompt: What are TypeScript conditional types used for?
